evolution of the Indian Constitution began with the Regulating Act, 1773 began British control over the Company and created the Governor-General of Bengal The Pitt’s India Act, 1784 introduced dual control of India through the British government The Charter Act, 1813 ended trade monopoly (except tea) and supported education The Charter Act, 1833 centralised administration and ended Company trade The Charter Act, 1853 introduced civil service competition and separated legislative and executive functions The Indian Councils Act, 1861 included Indians in councils by nomination The Indian Councils Act, 1892 expanded councils and introduced limited elections SOME IMPORTANT ACTS DURING BRITISH PERIOD IN INDIA Indian Councils Act, 1909 (Morley-Minto Reforms) (Separate Electorates Introduced)  Separate Electorates: For Muslims; start of communal politics  Elected Indians: Entry of elected Indians in legislative councils (First time indirect elections were introduced in India)  Executive Councils Expanded: Indian nominated to Viceroy's executive council (Satyendra Prasanna Sinha, he became the first Indian to enter the Viceroy’s Executive Council as Law Member) Government of India Act, 1919/Montague-Chelmsford Reforms (Dyarchy Introduced)  Indian Members in Executive Council:

Bhimrao Ambedkar noted, the Indian constitution is a living document, and it must evolve with the changing times, challenges, and aspirations of the nation If it isn't allowed to change, it could hinder the growth of the nation THE NECESSITY OF CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENTS  Evolving social order: Protect weaker sections and ensure social justice (e g , 106th Amendment, women’s reservation)  Strengthening institutions: Improve governance and political stability (e g , 52nd Amendment, Anti-Defection Law)  Technological changes: Address new issues like digital privacy and data protection  Fulfilling social contracts: Implement constitutional ideals like Gram Swaraj (73rd & 74th Amendments)  Structural adjustments: Modify fundamental provisions as per changing economic needs (e g , abolition of Right to Property) 

(UPSC 2019)  In Keshavnanda Bharti Case, the Supreme Court held that Parliament has the power to amend any part of the Constitution, including Fundamental Rights However, it ruled that this power is not unlimited and cannot be used to alter or destroy the 'Basic Structure' of the Constitution  Similarly, in the Minerva Mill case, the Supreme Court examined the validity of certain provisions of the 42nd Constitutional Amendment, which sought to enhance Parliament's powers to amend the Constitution It held that granting unlimited amending powers to Parliament would itself violate the Basic Structure of the Constitution Constitutional Amendments in India 5 The judgment reaffirmed the Basic Structure Doctrine and emphasized the importance of maintaining a balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles Thus, Parliament cannot use Article 368 to expand its powers in a way that damages the core values of the Constitution

to all Indian citizens, essential for a life of dignity and freedom They act as limitations on the power of the government, ensuring that the government cannot arbitrarily deny these rights to individuals These rights are guaranteed to all Indian citizens, irrespective of caste, religion, gender, or social status They are inspired from the Bill of Rights of the American Constitution FEATURES OF FUNDAMENTAL RIGHTS  Protection against arbitrary power of the State; ensures dignity, liberty, and minority protection  Justiciable and enforceable through courts via writs  Not absolute; subject to reasonable restrictions in public interest  Judicially dynamic; scope expanded through interpretations (e g , Right to Privacy under Article 21)  Emergency flexibility; some rights can be suspended, but Articles 20 and 21 remain protected ARTICLE 12  Article 12 defines ‘State’ for the purpose of Part III (Fundamental Rights) of the Constitution It includes: Central and State Governments (Executive and Legislature), Local Authorities (e g , Municipalities, Panchayats), Other Authorities (including statutory bodies and government- controlled institutions)  Judiciary & Article 12: The judiciary is excluded

Comptroller and Auditor General of India15 The Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG), appointed under Article 148 of the Indian Constitution, plays a crucial role in ensuring transparency and accountability in government finances The CAG’s independence is safeguarded by a fixed tenure of six years or until the age of 65, with removal only through a special parliamentary resolution The CAG audits Union and State government finances, submits reports to the President or Governor, and ensures legal compliance by disallowing improper expenditures It also sets accounting standards and advises the government on public finance matters, making it essential for fiscal responsibility and good governance (UPSC 2018) DUTIES AND POWER OF CAG These are laid down by the Parliament in the CAG (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971 CAG Audits following Government Accounts Constitutional Provisions For CAG  Central government expenditure from the Consolidated Fund of India

Dicey, it asserts that law governs a nation, ensuring that no individual or institution, including the government, is above it. Key Elements include- Supremacy of Law: Law is the highest authority. Federal System The Constitution of India establishes a federal system of government, although the term federation is not explicitly mentioned. Unlike the USA, Indian federalism did not arise from agreements among states; it is modelled after the Canadian system. The USA, the first and oldest federation in the world, was formed in 1787 following the American Revolution (1775–83). Federal Structure: India is described as a ‘Union of States’ (Article 1), reflecting its sociocultural diversity and large size. This structure allows for a quasi-federal system that accommodates regional autonomy while maintaining a strong central authority. Quasi-Federal: The federalism in India represents a compromise between the following two conflicting considerations: normal division of powers under which states enjoy autonomy within their own spheres; and need for national integrity and a strong Union government under exceptional circumstances. Supreme Court, High Court and Subordinate Courts The Indian Judicial System is an integrated and independent judicial framework established by the Constitution to uphold the rule of law, protect fundamental rights, and ensure the supremacy of the Constitution. India follows a single integrated judiciary, unlike the dual system in some federations, where the Supreme Court stands at the apex, followed by High Courts at the state level and subordinate courts at the district and lower levels. This integration ensures uniformity in the interpretation and application of laws throughout the country. Historical Background Of

Supreme Court stands at the apex, followed by High Courts at the state level and subordinate courts at the district and lower levels. This integration ensures uniformity in the interpretation and application of laws throughout the country. Historical Background Of The Indian Judiciary Regulating Act, 1773: Established the Supreme Court of Judicature in Calcutta (1774). Later, Supreme Courts were set up in Madras (1800) and Bombay (1823) under King George III. Indian High Courts Act, 1861: Created High Courts in provinces, abolishing Supreme Courts in Calcutta, Madras, Bombay and Sadar Adalats. These High Courts were the highest judicial bodies until the Federal Court of India was established under the Government of India Act, 1935 to resolve disputes between provinces and states. Post-Independence: After independence, existing High Courts for provinces became High Courts for states. The Seventh Amendment Act of 1956 allowed Parliament to create a common High Court for two or more states or union territories. allowed Parliament to create a common High Court for two or more states or union territories. Structure of the Indian Judiciary Integrated Judicial System: India has a unified judicial system where Central and State laws are enforced by the same courts. The Supreme Court is at the top, followed by High Courts and subordinate courts like District Courts. High Courts: The High Court is the highest court in a state, working under the Supreme Court. Established in 1862 for Calcutta, Bombay, Madras, and later Allahabad (1866). High Courts have jurisdiction over their respective states or combined states/union territories. There are currently 25 High Courts in India; the Calcutta High Court (1862) is the oldest. High Courts now have revenue jurisdiction, absent before the Constitution. Subordinate Courts: Each High Court oversees a hierarchy of subordinate courts, including District and Sessions Courts. fair. The Indian Constitution’s Part XV (Articles 324-329) lays down the provisions for conducting elections and establishes the Election Commission for this purpose. Basis: Representative democracy under the Constitution of India. Types of Elections A. Direct Elections Citizens directly vote for their representatives. Examples: o Lok Sabha members o State Legislative Assembly members o President of India (indirectly via electoral college, so partially direct) B. Indirect Elections Representatives are elected by elected members of another body. Examples: o Rajya Sabha (by MLAs) o President of India (by Electoral College) o Vice-President of India (by MPs) Features of Indian Elections 1. Universal Adult Franchise: All citizens above 18 years can vote (Article 326). 2. Free and Fair Elections: Ensured by Election Commission. 3. Regular Elections: Held at fixed intervals (5 years for Lok Sabha and Assemblies). 4. Secret Ballot: Voting is confidential. 5. Representation: Elections reflect people’s mandate. 6. Periodic & Direct/Indirect: Ensures continuity of democracy.
